dedupe_keys.name: archimedes screw pumps at the albert canal locks against low meuse discharge flanders belgium

description: This Climate-ADAPT case study describes how De Vlaamse Waterweg, the Flemish inland waterway manager, keeps the Albert Canal navigable when the Meuse, its water source, runs low. The canal links the industrial area of Liège with the port of Antwerp, and projections from the CORDEX.be project show deeper summer water deficits, with August rainfall falling by 10 to 40 percent by 2100. Large fish-friendly Archimedes screws were installed at the locks: four screws of 4.3 m diameter and 85 tonnes at Ham in 2012, then Olen in 2013 and Hasselt in 2018, with three more lock systems under way. In drought they pump the water lost in lock operations (48,000 m3 per operation, up to 5 m3 per second) back to the upper reach; with surplus water they generate hydropower, about ten months a year, equal to the use of 1,000 families per set. Each lock system costs about EUR 7 million, over a 40-year life. The measures followed a low-water strategy developed with industry, shipping, drinking water and nature stakeholders and assessed with a suite of models. The page, first published in 2016 and updated in 2026, is accessible online as free HTML. Caveats: the page gives no navigation or traffic figures, and the energy balance depends on rainfall, shipping and withdrawals. The case illustrates climate adaptation of inland waterway operations to drought; related records are the Rhine-Alpine inland freight data and the USACE National Waterway Network.
name: Archimedes screw pumps at the Albert Canal locks against low Meuse discharge, Flanders, Belgium
outcomes: Screw pumps at Ham (2012), Olen (2013) and Hasselt (2018) return lock water in droughts and generate hydropower about ten months a year, keeping the canal navigable at about EUR 7 million per lock system.
provider: Climate-ADAPT (European Environment Agency), case study from the Flemish Government and De Vlaamse Waterweg
